Verdict: ACCEPTThe general local-stability theorem, its fixed- $S$  adaptive refinement, and its bounded-degree composition corollaries are valid as supplied. No mathematical correction or checker-source change is required.I extracted all four embedded files without changing their bytes, verified every manifest hash, compiled and ran the unchanged C++17 checker with checks active, and obtained a report byte-for-byte identical to the supplied 622-byte report. The proof assessment below is independent of that computational result and of the research-stage response.The complete findings, unchanged inputs, executable, generated report, compilation and execution records, and checksums are in    local-stability-audit.zip.1. Radius-three preservation is correct for each original witnessThe delicate part of Lemma 2 is valid in arbitrary finite simple graphs. It preserves the same original deletion witness, not merely the existence of some witness.Fix  $v\in S$  and an original deletion witness  $x$ . If  $x\ne v$ , every former forming star at  $x$  must contain  $v$ ; otherwise that star would survive deleting  $v$ . Therefore
$$\operatorname{dist}_G(v,x)\le 2.$$
The proof covers every way that adding  $A$  can destroy this witness: $x=v$  becomes formed. Its new star must contain an added selection; otherwise it would already have been formed after deleting  $v$ . This puts  $A$  within distance two of  $v$ . $x\in A$ . The witness disappears because it becomes selected. Its old star gives distance at most two from  $v$  to  $A$ . $x$  remains outside the enlarged selection. A new forming star must use  $A$ . If  $vx$  is an edge, or if an added vertex in the new star is adjacent to  $x$ , the old and new star distances give distance at most three from  $v$  to  $A$ .The remaining case. The old star is  $x-w-v$ , and the new star is  $x-t-a$ , with  $w,t\in S\setminus\{v\}$  and  $a\in A$ . If  $w\ne t$ , then  $x$  already had two selected neighbours after deleting  $v$ , contradicting its failure. If  $w=t$ , the path  $v-w-a$  has length two.That last case is exactly what improves a naive radius-four argument to radius three. It is exhaustive. Extra edges, including triangles, do not cause a problem because the stars are not required to be induced.The stated local premise is also correct: for an outside witness  $x\ne v$ , the argument needs formation before deletion only at  $x$ . For a self-witness  $x=v$ , it needs no original outside-formation premise. This distinction supports the reverse argument.    Source: local proof, §1.2. The adaptive canonical repair and its universal retention claim are validFor  $H=G-U$ , define  $S_H=S\setminus U$  and let  $A$  be exactly the outside vertices of  $H$  unformed by  $S_H$ .Every  $x\in A$  was outside the original  $S$ . Its old forming star must contain a selected vertex of  $U$ , since otherwise both selected vertices and their edges would survive in the induced graph  $H$ . Thus
$$A\subseteq B_2(U).$$
Selecting  $A$  repairs formation: previously formed outside vertices retain their stars, while the failed vertices become selected.Now take
$$v\in C:=S_H\setminus\bigl(B_2(U)\cup B_3(A)\bigr).$$
For any original witness  $x$  of  $v$ :The witness survives deleting  $U$ . If  $x\ne v$ , its distance at most two from  $v$  excludes  $x\in U$ . If  $x=v$ , survival follows from  $v\in S_H$ .Adding  $A$  does not destroy it. Lemma 2 applies because  $v\notin B_3(A)$ . This also excludes the possibility that the witness becomes selected into  $A$ .Removing  $U$  cannot create a star. Hence the same surviving outside vertex remains unformed in  $H$  after deleting  $v$  from the repaired selection.Therefore  $v$  is essential even in  $S_H\cup A$ . The stronger claim about every minimal forming subset follows: any forming subset omitting  $v$  would be contained in the known nonforming set  $(S_H\cup A)\setminus\{v\}$ , contradicting upward closure.A minimal forming subset exists by finiteness, so  $|C|\le SF_2(H)$ . Decomposing  $S$  then gives exactly the supplied fixed- $S$  inequality:
$$|S|
\le SF_2(H)+|S\cap U|
+\left|S_H\cap\bigl(B_2(U)\cup B_3(A)\bigr)\right|.$$
Finally,  $A\subseteq B_2(U)$  implies  $B_3(A)\subseteq B_5(U)$ . Choosing an  $SF_2(G)$ -maximizing  $S$  gives the numerical upper bound. There is no assumption that the original restriction  $S_H$  is forming or minimal.    Source: local proof, Theorem 1 and §2.3. The reverse bound does not require  $T$  to form all of  $G$ This potential gap is explicitly avoided.Let  $T$  be a maximum minimal forming set of  $H$ . For a deletion witness  $x\in H$ , the graph induced by
$$(T\setminus\{v\})\cup\{x\}$$
is identical whether considered in  $H$  or in  $G$ . Consequently, its failure before adding  $U$  is identical in both graphs. If  $x\ne v$ , its original forming star in  $H$  is also present in  $G$ .These are precisely the pointwise hypotheses used by Lemma 2. Whether vertices of  $U$  are initially formed by  $T$  is irrelevant.The set  $T\cup U$  does form  $G$ . Every  $v\in T\setminus B_3(U)$  retains its old witness after selecting  $U$ , so every forming subset of  $T\cup U$  contains those vertices. Minimal extraction therefore gives
$$SF_2(G)\ge |T\setminus B_3(U)|
\ge SF_2(H)-b_3(U).$$
No hidden global-forming hypothesis is needed.    Source: local proof, §2, lower-bound argument.4. Both  $P_9$  certificates are correct—and have the stated scopeFor  $P_9$  on  $0,\ldots,8$ , take
$$S=\{0,1,4,5,6,8\}.$$
The outside vertices  $2,3,7$  are formed through the selected edges  $1-0$ ,  $4-5$ , and the selected neighbours  $6,8$ , respectively.I checked every displayed deletion witness:Deleted vertexWitnessWhy it fails after deletion $0$  $0$ Its sole selected neighbour  $1$  becomes inactive. $1$  $1$ Its sole selected neighbour  $0$  becomes inactive. $4$  $3$ No selected neighbour remains. $5$  $3$ Its sole selected neighbour  $4$  becomes inactive. $6$  $7$ Its sole selected neighbour  $8$  is inactive. $8$  $8$ No selected neighbour remains.After adding  $2$  and deleting  $5$ , the selection is
$$\{0,1,2,4,6,8\}.$$
Each outside vertex  $3,5,7$  has two selected neighbours. Thus  $5$  becomes deletable at distance exactly three from the added selection.After deleting  $U=\{0\}$ , the restricted selection fails exactly at  $2$ , so the canonical repair is  $A=\{2\}$ . Deleting  $5$  after repair leaves
$$\{1,2,4,6,8\},$$
again forming all outside vertices  $3,5,7$ . Since  $\operatorname{dist}(5,U)=5$ , a minimal forming subset omitting  $5$  exists.These examples establish the claimed sharpness of the certificate-preservation thresholds: strictly greater than three for additions, and strictly greater than five for canonical repair. They do not establish optimal numerical error bounds for  $SF_2$ , and the note correctly makes that distinction.    Source: local proof, §3.5. The square-ear dependencies and BFS coefficient are correctSupplying square-ear theoremThe two dependencies used by the local corollary pass review:Exactly two selections per square. With fewer than two, an interior vertex remains unformed. With three or four, the proposed internal deletion forms the newly omitted vertex and retains the activity of every selected root, preserving outside formation.The lower lift is minimal. Selecting all new interior pairs together with a minimal forming set of  $F$ , while leaving roots unselected, forms the roots and preserves every old core deletion witness. No new selected vertex is adjacent to  $F$ . Deleting a selected interior vertex has the stated local self-witness.I checked all six selected-pair rows and all twelve deletion witnesses in the square table. Arbitrary old-old edges cannot rescue these witnesses: the relevant failure has either no selected neighbour or a sole inactive interior neighbour. This includes triangles and edges between roots of different squares.    Source: square-ear proof, §§2–3.Distance and countingLet  $U$  be the union of all four-vertex ear-squares. Matching edges make these squares vertex-disjoint, so every minimal forming set satisfies
$$|S\cap U|=2k.$$
For  $x\in F$ ,
$$\operatorname{dist}_G(x,U)=\operatorname{dist}_B(x,R).$$
A path from  $F$  must first enter  $U$  at an old root; its initial segment is entirely in the base. Conversely, a base path to  $R$  reaches  $U$ . This also handles infinite distances.The fixed- $S$  inequality, applied to a maximizing  $S$ , therefore yields
$$0\le SF_2(G)-\bigl(2k+SF_2(F)\bigr)
\le \left|\{x\in F:\operatorname{dist}_B(x,R)\le5\}\right|.$$
To verify the exact coefficient, write
$$L_j=\{x\in F:\operatorname{dist}_B(x,R)=j\}.$$
Each of the  $2k$  roots has two mandatory, distinct neighbours outside  $F$ : its matched root and its new interior neighbour. Therefore
$$|L_1|\le 2k(\Delta-2).$$
Every subsequent layer vertex has a predecessor, leaving at most  $\Delta-1$  forward neighbours. Hence
$$|L_j|\le 2k(\Delta-2)(\Delta-1)^{j-1},
\qquad 1\le j\le5.$$
Summing gives precisely
$$\boxed{2k(\Delta-2)\sum_{j=0}^{4}(\Delta-1)^j}.$$
Overlapping neighbourhoods, repeated predecessors, triangles, same-layer edges, and extra root-root edges only reduce the number of distinct vertices counted. The base-degree variant
$$2k\sum_{j=1}^{5}(\delta-1)^j$$
is also correct: a root has at most  $\delta-1$  core neighbours, and the later forward factor is again  $\delta-1$ .    Source: local proof, §§4–5.6.
